title: 1 Kings 10:1–13
context: This passage is kept whole. The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame concerning the LORD’s name and comes to test him with hard questions, bringing a great caravan of spices, gold and precious stones. Solomon answers everything. Seeing his wisdom, his house, his table and his ascent to the LORD’s house, she is overwhelmed. She confesses that the report was true and that she had not heard the half of it, and she blesses the LORD, who loved Israel and made Solomon king to do justice and righteousness. She gives lavish gifts, Hiram’s fleet brings almug wood and precious stones, and Solomon gives her all she desires before she returns home. Sheba is commonly associated with southwestern Arabia, though some traditions link the queen with East Africa; the location is not certain. Jesus later points to the queen of the south who came from far away to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and says that something greater than Solomon is here (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31). Both traditions read the account as narrative of God-given wisdom drawing the nations, not as an allegory with a doctrinal fork.

verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the LORD’s name, she came to test him with hard questions.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame concerning the LORD’s name, she comes to test him with hard questions. His reputation is tied to the LORD.

Arminian readers note that the queen responds freely to what she has heard, and that God’s blessing on Israel was meant to draw the nations to seek the truth, as the dedication prayer hoped (8:41–43).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Solomon’s fame is explicitly linked to the LORD’s name, so that the queen’s journey ultimately points beyond Solomon to the God who gave him wisdom (3:12). Sheba is commonly associated with southwestern Arabia, though this is not certain.

Both traditions see her coming as a sign of God’s blessing reaching the nations.

verses.text: She came to Jerusalem with a very great caravan, with camels that bore spices, very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him about all that was in her heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
She arrives in Jerusalem with a very great caravan of camels carrying spices, much gold and precious stones, and talks with Solomon about all that is on her heart. Her visit is both diplomatic and personal.

Arminian readers note that the queen comes with genuine questions, and that honest seeking is welcomed; she speaks freely about all that is in her heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the wealth she brings fits the picture of the nations bringing their treasures to Israel’s king, a theme later prophets develop (compare Isaiah 60:6), though the narrative here is first a historical account. Trade between the regions may also lie behind the visit.

Both traditions read her open conversation with Solomon as a fitting response to God-given wisdom.

verses.text: Solomon answered all her questions. There wasn’t anything hidden from the king which he didn’t tell her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon answers all her questions; nothing is hidden from the king that he does not explain to her. His wisdom is complete for her purposes.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s wisdom is a gift he shares generously, and that God’s gifts are given not only for their recipient but for the blessing of others who seek understanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the wisdom on display is the gift God promised at Gibeon (3:12), so that every answer Solomon gives testifies to God’s faithfulness to his word rather than to Solomon’s native brilliance.

Both traditions agree that the wisdom displayed here is God’s gift, and that it serves to make God known.

verses.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,
verses.arminianNotes:
When the queen has seen all Solomon’s wisdom and the house he built, she begins to take in what is before her. Seeing confirms hearing.

Arminian readers note that the queen’s experience moves from report to personal observation, and that faith often grows as people come and see for themselves what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the house Solomon built may refer to his palace or include the temple, and that the queen observes the visible order of a kingdom blessed by God, which the following verse details.

Both traditions read the verse as the beginning of her recognition that the report she heard was true.

verses.text: the food of his table, the sitting of his servants, the attendance of his officials, their clothing, his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to the LORD’s house, there was no more spirit in her.
verses.arminianNotes:
She sees the food of his table, his servants’ seating, his officials’ attendance and clothing, his cupbearers, and his ascent to the LORD’s house, and she is left breathless. The WEB says there was no more spirit in her.

Arminian readers note that the queen is overwhelmed by the beauty and order of Solomon’s court, and that such splendor can stir wonder that leads toward the God behind it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the list climaxes with Solomon’s ascent to the LORD’s house, which some translations render as the burnt offerings he offered there; either way, worship crowns the scene.

Both traditions see the queen’s amazement as a response to God’s blessing visibly displayed in Solomon’s kingdom.

verses.text: She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts and of your wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
She tells the king that the report she heard in her own land about his acts and wisdom was true. She confirms what she was told.

Arminian readers note that the queen’s honest confession shows a willingness to have her skepticism corrected by evidence, and that God honors sincere seekers who follow the truth where it leads.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that her testimony confirms the truth of the report about Solomon, which itself was a report about the LORD’s blessing, so that her words become a witness to God’s faithfulness before the nations.

Both traditions read her confession as genuine and fitting.

verses.text: However, I didn’t believe the words until I came and my eyes had seen it. Behold, not even half was told me! Your wisdom and prosperity exceed the fame which I heard.
verses.arminianNotes:
She says she did not believe the reports until she came and saw, and not even half had been told her; his wisdom and prosperity exceed what she heard. Reality surpasses reputation.

Arminian readers note that her initial unbelief gave way when she came and saw, and that God often meets honest doubt by revealing more than was expected.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the queen’s words highlight the abundance of God’s gifts, which exceed human report, and many Christians in both traditions hear an echo in Jesus’ words that someone greater than Solomon has come (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31).

Both traditions see her experience as a picture of God’s goodness exceeding expectation.

verses.text: Happy are your men, happy are these your servants who stand continually before you, who hear your wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
She says that Solomon’s men and servants who stand before him continually and hear his wisdom are happy. She envies their privilege.

Arminian readers note that the queen recognizes the blessing of daily access to wisdom, and that those who live near God’s gifts should value them rather than take them for granted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the blessing of standing before the king and hearing his wisdom anticipates the greater privilege of those who hear Christ, to whom Jesus pointed when he spoke of the queen (Luke 11:31), though the verse is first about Solomon’s court.

Both traditions read her words as an invitation to treasure wisdom.

verses.text: Blessed is the LORD your God, who delighted in you, to set you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD loved Israel forever, therefore he made you king, to do justice and righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She blesses the LORD Solomon’s God, who delighted in him and set him on Israel’s throne; because the LORD loved Israel forever, he made him king to do justice and righteousness. She praises Israel’s God.

Arminian readers note that the queen ties Solomon’s kingship to a purpose, justice and righteousness, which the king is responsible to carry out, and that God’s gifts come with a calling.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that she grounds Solomon’s reign in the LORD’s delight and everlasting love for Israel, so that the king’s position rests on God’s gracious choice rather than his own merit.

Both traditions agree that the purpose of kingship is justice and righteousness, and that the queen’s praise rightly honors the LORD.

verses.text: She gave the king one hundred twenty talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again was there such an abundance of spices as these which the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
She gives the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold, a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones; never again was there such an abundance of spices. Her gifts are lavish.

Arminian readers note that generous giving is a natural response to blessing received, and that the queen’s gifts express gratitude and honor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the gifts of the nations flowing to Israel’s king fit the larger biblical picture of the nations honoring God’s anointed, a theme many Christians see fulfilled in the gifts brought to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11), though the text does not make that link.

Both traditions read the gifts as a sign of God’s blessing on Solomon’s kingdom.

verses.text: The fleet of Hiram that brought gold from Ophir also brought in from Ophir great quantities of almug trees and precious stones.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram’s fleet, which brought gold from Ophir, also brings large quantities of almug wood and precious stones. The WEB footnote suggests almug may be an Indian sandalwood.

Arminian readers note that the narrator interrupts the queen’s story to show other sources of Solomon’s wealth, emphasizing that blessing flowed from many directions during his reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the exact identity of almug wood is uncertain, as the footnote’s possibly indicates, and that the narrative’s interest lies in the rare and costly materials gathered for the LORD’s house and the palace.

Both traditions read the notice descriptively and hold the identification lightly.

verses.text: The king made of the almug trees pillars for the LORD’s house and for the king’s house, harps also and stringed instruments for the singers; no such almug trees came or were seen to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king uses the almug wood for supports in the LORD’s house and the king’s house, and for harps and lyres for the singers; no such almug wood came again. The wood serves worship.

Arminian readers note that Solomon puts rare materials to use in worship and music, showing that the best of what God provides is fittingly given back to his service.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that music for the LORD’s house was an important part of worship in Israel, as Chronicles stresses, and that the finest gifts of creation are rightly devoted to the praise of God. The exact meaning of the word rendered pillars is uncertain.

Both traditions see the use of the almug wood in worship as fitting.

verses.text: King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked, in addition to that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own land, she and her servants.
verses.arminianNotes:
King Solomon gives the queen all she desires and asks for, besides what he gives from his royal bounty, and she returns to her land with her servants. The visit ends in generosity.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s generosity matches the queen’s, and that the exchange of gifts reflects mutual honor between nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the queen returns home having seen the blessing of the LORD on Israel, and that the narrative leaves her story with her blessing of the LORD in verse 9 echoing in the reader’s mind; the text does not say what she did after returning.

Both traditions read the account as narrative, honoring God’s wisdom and generosity without allegorizing it into a doctrinal fork.
